subject: Banking
title: Subprime: Lending to Lose
description: A 60-second lesson on Subprime: Lending to Lose.

hook.text: Banks gave mortgages to people who couldn't repay them, then sold those mortgages as 'safe' investments.

buildup.text: Subprime lenders offered 'teaser' rates: 1-2% for two years, then jumping to 8-10%.

discovery.text: Countrywide Financial originated $97 billion in subprime loans in one year. Volume meant commissions.

twist.text: Loan officers earned commissions for every loan closed, regardless of repayment.

climax.text: Subprime lending wasn't just risky. It was designed to extract fees from people who couldn't afford the terms.

punchline.text: $97 billion in bad loans. Designed to collect fees, not to be repaid.

quiz.question: Why did banks issue subprime mortgages to people who couldn't repay?
options: Loan officers earned commissions per loan regardless of repayment

details.summary: Banks deliberately issued mortgages to borrowers who could not afford them, knowing the loans would default, because packaging and selling these toxic loans as securities generated immediate fees and bonuses.
details.whyItMatters: Subprime lending destroyed millions of families' financial lives and triggered the 2008 global recession. Banks profited from origination while passing the risk to investors and ultimately to taxpayers.
takeaways: Banks issued no-documentation NINJA loans to unqualified borrowers
Loan officers were incentivized by volume, not quality
The resulting defaults triggered the worst financial crisis since the 1930s

faq.question: What were NINJA loans?
faq.answer: NINJA stood for No Income, No Job, No Assets. Banks issued mortgages to people without verifying employment, income, or savings. The loans were designed to be sold off quickly so the originator bore no default risk.

faq.question: Why did banks make loans they knew would fail?
faq.answer: Banks earned fees immediately upon origination and again when selling the loans as securities. Since the risk was passed to investors, the bank's profit was locked in regardless of whether borrowers could ever repay.
